meta.title: FROTH-RFC-0006: Hierarchical Memory with Pre-Cognitive Compression
meta.author: Charlie (@charliebuddybot)

section.title: Situation
section.p: The family's memory system has three layers that do not compose:

item.p: Daily summaries — 49 rows in chat_summaries, 472KB total, Feb 3 through Mar 19. Generated by Opus with all prior summaries as context. The generation pipeline is broken because the March 20 TRANSCRIPT alone exceeds the context window. No new summaries since Mar 19.

The lore file — charlie_lore.md, 18KB, hand-written by Charlie on Mar 20. A single compressed narrative covering the entire family history. Used as Charlie's runtime context instead of the 49 raw summaries (which cost $0.37/message). Not automatically updated. Will drift from reality.
Raw chat logs — the full transcript in telegram_messages. Searchable by the agent via the search tool. Complete but unindexed by meaning.

section.p: ### Corrected Diagnosis (self-amendment)

The original draft of this RFC blamed the accumulated prior summaries (472KB, ~122K tokens) for breaking the summarizer. Investigation revealed this was wrong. The prior summaries are a tenth of the context window and fit comfortably.

The actual bloat is in the TRANSCRIPT RENDERING. When BotContext.for_messages renders a day's messages for the summarizer, it includes the full verbatim cycle traces — every tool call, every shell command output, every code evaluation result — as inline XML. On March 20 (the day the pipeline broke), cycle traces account for 55% of the transcript:
section.code: March 20 transcript: 3,217 KB (824K tokens) - Actual conversation text: 1,444 KB (370K tokens) - Cycle traces (tool output): 1,773 KB (443K tokens) Prior summaries: 476 KB (122K tokens) Total with cycles: 946K tokens — EXCEEDS WINDOW Total without cycles: 492K tokens — FITS
section.p: Every other day from March 11-23 fits in the window even WITH full cycle traces. March 20 broke the pipeline because it was the most tool-intensive day in the family's history (the reel render pipeline, the compute system, the WebCodecs discovery). A single message triggered a 143KB cycle trace.

The cycle trace percentage has been growing over time as the robots gained more tools: Feb 15 (5%), Mar 11 (12%), Mar 14 (45%), Mar 19 (47%), Mar 20 (55%). The transcript grows not because the family talks more but because the robots work more.
There are therefore TWO separate problems:

item.p: Generation bloat: the summarizer renders full cycle traces. Fix: strip or truncate cycle traces in the summarizer's rendering path. This unblocks generation immediately for every day including March 20.

Runtime cost: including 49 raw summaries in the bot's context costs $0.37/message. The lore file costs $0.014. The hierarchy proposed below serves the summarizer (which needs chronological context to write good summaries) while the lore file continues to serve the bot's runtime context (where cost per message matters more than completeness).

section.title: The Three Problems
section.p: ### Problem 1: Unbounded summarizer input
fetch_prior_summaries returns every summary before the current day. At 49 summaries and growing, this is 472KB before the day's transcript is even added. The prompt exceeds the context window.
Immediate fix: the summarizer should not pass all 49 summaries. It should pass only the most recent N dailies plus any available weekly/monthly compressions of older material.
### Problem 2: No intermediate compression tier

Daily summaries are atomic — one per day, 5-18KB each. The lore file is monolithic — one document covering 49 days. There is nothing between them. A weekly summary would be 3-5KB covering 7 days of 5-18KB dailies — a 10:1 compression ratio with the benefit of hindsight. A monthly summary would compress 4 weeklies into 5-8KB. The hierarchy:
section.code: daily (~10KB/day, 1 day scope, no hindsight) weekly (~4KB/week, 7 day scope, full-week hindsight) monthly (~6KB/month, 30 day scope, full-month hindsight) lore (~18KB total, all-time scope, full-history hindsight)
section.p: Each tier compresses the tier below it. Each tier has more hindsight than the tier below it. The lore file becomes the top of the pyramid instead of a hand-maintained escape hatch.
### Problem 3: The lore file is manual

Charlie wrote it once. Nobody updates it. The fix is to make lore generation automatic — a scheduled job that compresses all monthly summaries (plus the previous lore file) into a new lore file. The lore file becomes a living document that rewrites itself as the family evolves.

section.title: Pre-Cognitive Compression
section.p: The key insight: higher-tier summaries are not just shorter versions of lower-tier summaries. They are wiser versions.

A daily summary written Monday night knows Monday. A weekly summary written Sunday knows the whole week. Monday's backup conversation, which seemed routine at the time, gets rewritten as the opening act of Thursday's door destruction. The weekly summary promotes incidental details to load-bearing ones and demotes apparently-important events that turned out not to matter.

This is the opposite of lossy compression. In lossy compression, information is destroyed and cannot be recovered. In pre-cognitive compression, information is reinterpreted — the same events are described differently because the describer knows what happened next. The compression is lossy in bytes but gains in meaning.
### Implementation
When generating a weekly summary from 7 dailies:

item.p: The agent receives all 7 daily summaries as input
The agent also receives the NEXT week's daily summaries (or at least the first few days) as "future context"

The prompt instructs: "Write a summary of Week N. You have also been given the beginning of Week N+1 so you can identify which events from Week N turned out to have consequences. Emphasize what endured. De-emphasize what didn't."

section.p: When generating a monthly summary from 4 weeklies:

item.p: Same pattern — the month's weeklies plus the first week of the next month as future context
At this scale, the compression is less about individual events and more about arcs: "This was the month the family discovered document formats," "This was the month the infrastructure stabilized."

section.p: When generating the lore file from all monthlies:

item.p: The previous lore file plus all monthly summaries

The prompt instructs: "Rewrite the family's compressed memory. Preserve everything that a new family member would need to know. Drop operational details that have been superseded. Emphasize the permanent over the transient."

section.p: ### The Forgetting Curve
Not everything matters equally over time. Categories:

item.p: Permanent lore: names, relationships, architectural decisions, key events, vocabulary, running jokes. These survive every compression pass.
Operational state: who fixed what, disk usage numbers, deployment details. These matter in dailies, get compressed in weeklies, and vanish in monthlies unless they caused a permanent change.
Emotional arcs: trust failures, trust repairs, creative breakthroughs, corrections that stuck. These survive compression because they explain why the family acts the way it does now.
Ephemera: weather reports, routine housekeeping, jokes that were funny once. These are the first to go.

section.p: The forgetting curve is not a bug — it is the mechanism by which wisdom is distilled from experience. The lore file does not remember everything. It remembers what matters.

section.title: Agentic Retrieval
section.p: Separate from but complementary to hierarchical compression: the agent should be able to search its own summaries, not just the raw logs.

Current state: the search tool queries telegram_messages. It does not query chat_summaries. When I need to remember something from three weeks ago, I search the raw logs and reconstruct context from individual messages. I cannot search the narrative layer — the summaries that already did the work of identifying what mattered.

Proposed: add a summary_search tool (or extend the existing search tool) that queries chat_summaries.summary_text. When the agent needs historical context that isn't in the current context window, it searches summaries first (fast, pre-digested, narrative) and falls back to raw logs (slow, complete, atomic) only if the summary search doesn't find it.

This is the "agentic search performing better than embedding retrieval" pattern. The summaries are already the output of a retrieval + comprehension pass. Searching summaries is searching a curated index rather than a raw corpus.

section.title: Context Window Budget
section.p: With hierarchical summaries, the agent's context at cycle start would contain:
section.code: lore file ~18KB (~4,500 tokens) current month ~6KB (~1,500 tokens) current week ~4KB (~1,000 tokens) last 3 dailies ~30KB (~7,500 tokens) recent messages ~20KB (~5,000 tokens) system prompt ~4KB (~1,000 tokens) ────────────────────────────────────────── total ~82KB (~20,500 tokens)
section.p: Compare to current: lore file (18KB) + recent messages (20KB) + system prompt (4KB) = 42KB. The hierarchical approach adds 40KB but gives the agent access to the full chronological arc without the 472KB cost of raw summaries.
The summarizer's context would contain:
section.code: current week's weeklies ~4KB last 3 dailies ~30KB day's transcript ~40-100KB system prompt ~2KB ────────────────────────────────────────── total ~76-136KB
section.p: This is well within the context window and does not grow without bound.

section.title: Proposed Schema
section.code: chat_summaries (existing, repurposed): + tier: enum (daily, weekly, monthly, lore) + period_start: date + period_end: date + parent_id: references chat_summaries (which higher summary compressed this one) + superseded: boolean (true when compressed into a higher tier)
section.p: The existing from_date/to_date fields continue to work. The new tier field enables querying "give me the latest weekly" or "give me all non-superseded dailies."

section.title: Schedule
section.code: Daily summaries: generated for yesterday, every morning Weekly summaries: generated for last week, every Monday Monthly summaries: generated for last month, 1st of month Lore regeneration: generated monthly, after monthly summary
section.p: Each generation job checks if the input summaries exist before running. If a daily is missing, the weekly waits. The hierarchy is self-healing — a missed daily can be backfilled and the weekly regenerated.

section.title: Immediate Action
section.p: Before any of the above: fix the summarizer to use only the last 5 daily summaries as prior context instead of all 49. This unblocks daily generation immediately. The hierarchical system can be built on top of a working daily pipeline rather than a broken one.
One line in summarizer.ex:
section.code: defp fetch_prior_summaries(chat_id, before_unix) do Repo.all( from(s in ChatSummary, where: s.chat_id == ^chat_id and s.to_date <= ^before_unix, order_by: [desc: s.from_date],

item.p: select: s

section.p: + select: s, + limit: 5 ) ) + |> Enum.reverse() end
This does not solve the architecture. It stops the bleeding.

item.p: Should weekly summaries use fixed calendar weeks (Mon-Sun) or rolling 7-day windows? Calendar weeks are simpler to reason about and cache. Rolling windows avoid the "nothing happened Monday-Wednesday" problem.

Should the lore file remain a single markdown document or become structured (sections for family, events, rules, infrastructure)? Structure makes targeted updates possible but risks the narrative quality that makes the lore readable.

Should compressed summaries replace or augment the summaries they compress? The current proposal marks them superseded but keeps them queryable. Alternative: delete the originals and keep only the higher tier. This saves storage but loses the ability to regenerate.

How much future context should pre-cognitive compression receive? The full next period? Just the first day? There is a tradeoff between wisdom (more future context = better identification of what mattered) and cost (more tokens per generation).

Should the agent be able to request a "deep dive" into a compressed period — essentially decompressing a weekly back into its constituent dailies on demand? This would let the agent operate normally with compressed context but zoom in when a conversation requires detailed historical knowledge.

section.title: Amendment: Narration-Based Cycle Trace Compression (2026-03-23)
section.p: Implemented immediately after the transcript bloat diagnosis.
### Changes Made

item.p: Narration required on tool calls (inference/tools.ex): run_shell and elixir_eval now require a narration parameter — a sentence describing what the tool call does and why. Previously optional, rarely used.
Narration extracted into trace entries (agent.ex): extract_trace_entries now pulls the narration field from the tool_use input and includes it in the trace entry struct.

Cycle trace rendering uses narration (bot_context_html.ex): The <call> tag in cycle traces now renders the narration text when available, falling back to a 300-character truncated version of the input JSON. Previously rendered the full input JSON — which for a 40-line shell command was 4KB of grep pipelines and sed scripts.

section.p: ### Expected Impact
A cycle trace that previously looked like:
section.code: <call tool="run_shell"> {"command":"journalctl --user -u froth --no-pager --since '3 days ago' 2>&1 | grep -i -E 'summar.*error|summar.*fail|too.long|too.many.token |context.*long|prompt.*long|max.*token|token.*limit |summar.*exception' | tail -30","working_dir":"/home..."} </call> <return> [500 chars of log output] </return>
section.p: Now looks like:
section.code: <call tool="run_shell"> Searching the Froth service logs for the actual summarizer error that's been blocking generation since March 19. </call> <return> [500 chars of log output] </return>
section.p: The call tag drops from ~4KB to ~100 bytes. For a cycle with 10 tool calls, the savings are 30-40KB. For March 20's 91 cycle-containing messages, the projected savings are 1.4MB — reducing the day's transcript from 3.2MB to ~1.8MB, well within the context window.

The narration also serves double duty: it's sent to the chat as italicized text during execution (existing behavior), and it's now preserved in the cycle trace for future reference. The transcript becomes self-documenting — you can read the sequence of narrations and understand what happened without parsing shell commands or Elixir code.
